title: The Note in the Glovebox
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 35 of 40
content:
The glovebox would not close.

Greg had spent ten minutes trying to make the map fit around an old flashlight, three receipts, a packet of guitar picks, and a folded piece of paper I had never seen before.

"What's that?" I asked.

He froze for half a second.

"Old stuff."

"Do you want help sorting it?"

"Maybe."

I didn't reach for the paper.

We were parked near Beach City, waiting for the rain to ease before driving up to the overlook. The inside of the van smelled of warm vinyl and the faint salt of years spent beside the ocean. Greg opened the glovebox again and lifted out the folded note.

"I wrote this a long time ago," he said.

"To who?"

"Myself, mostly."

He handed it to me.

"Would you like me to read it?" I asked.

"Yeah."

The note was short. It said that if he ever had a home worth coming back to, he should stop pretending he had to leave first. The words were clumsy and heartfelt. It had no signature except his name, written so hard the pen had marked the paper beneath.

I read it twice.

"When did you write it?"

"After one of the times I was pretty sure everything good was about to fall apart."

He looked at the dashboard.

"I didn't know what to do with it. I stuck it in here and kept finding it every time I tried to clean."

I felt a sharp ache in my chest.

"Why didn't you throw it away?"

"Because I kept thinking maybe someday I'd read it and know what it meant."

I folded the paper along its old creases.

"Do you know now?"

"Some days."

He looked at me.

"Other days I still get scared I have to be the funniest guy in the room, the one everybody can count on, or the one nobody asks too much of. Then I see the note and remember I wanted to stop running."

I handed it back.

"I don't want to be the reason you stop traveling."

"I know."

"I want you to choose when to come back."

He laughed softly.

"That sounds a lot harder."

"It is."

The rain softened. We carried the old map into a small roadside shelter because the van was too cramped for both of us to spread it across our knees. The paper had marks for places Greg wanted to visit when he was younger, many of them crossed out for reasons he'd forgotten.

"Did you ever go here?" I asked, pointing to a town on the coast.

"No. Ran out of gas money before I got there."

"Do you still want to?"

He considered.

"Maybe. Not because I owe it to that guy who wrote the list. Because it looks nice."

I took my own notebook from my bag, the one where I tracked voluntary Threadway visits to Lanternweald and the dates I'd promised people.

"Want to make a new map?"

"With actual plans?"

"Some actual plans. Some places we might visit. No promises we can't keep."

He liked that.

Greg tapped the date with his pencil.

"I told Nola I'd play forty minutes," he said. "Not the whole night. She's got other performers coming."

"Good."

"What if she asks me to stay for cleanup?"

"Then you decide whether you're available. Not whether you're a bad person if you leave."

He turned the pencil between his fingers.

"I used to think leaving was the worst thing I could do to someone. Then I got good at leaving before they asked."

I looked toward the van, where the old note had lived for years.

"Maybe there's a difference between abandoning somebody and finishing what you agreed to do."

He considered that.

"Forty minutes of music," he said. "And I can still help pack my own gear."

"That's a plan."

We added the return route and the last safe Threadway crossing we knew about. I wrote a question mark beside the time because the Lanternweald tide board could change after heavy rain.

Greg looked at the mark.

"You're okay with not knowing yet?"

"I am if we say that it's uncertain. I don't want to pretend we know something just because the blank part makes us uncomfortable."

He smiled.

"You'd get along with the people in the archive."

"Some of them are unbearable."

"And you love them anyway."

I looked at him.

"Yes."

He accepted the answer without needing it softened. Then he drew a star beside the concert and let the rest of the map remain unfinished.

We marked the next scheduled trip to Starwake Pier, where he had agreed to play a short concert. He wrote a reminder to check whether the stage was available and whether anyone else had already booked it.

Then he pointed to a town on the old map.

"Could we put that one down as a maybe?"

"Absolutely."

We added a little question mark.

He smiled.

"I like the maybe."

"Me too."

We sat quietly for a while, watching rain slide down the shelter roof.

"Can I ask something?" he said.

"Yes."

"Do you ever worry that leaving for another person means I'm going to stop wanting you back?"

I thought about it.

"Sometimes I worry you'll interpret my leaving as a judgment about you. But I've told you I'm ethically non-monogamous and prefer polyamory. We both chose this with our eyes open. The answer isn't to stop having other relationships. It's to keep asking what we actually want."

He considered.

"And what do you want today?"

"To finish this map. Then get dinner with you. Then maybe go home and forget the map for a while."

He laughed.

"Very romantic."

"Terribly."

He moved closer.

"Can I kiss you?"

"Yes."

We kissed under the shelter roof while the rain dwindled to a mist. He tasted like coffee, and I felt him smile when I wrapped my arms around him.

Before leaving the shelter, Greg opened the map again and drew three symbols beside Starwake Pier.

“Lightning bolt?” I asked.

“Power for the stage.”

“Rectangle?”

“Room for the equipment.”

“That... potato?”

“Bathroom. You'd be amazed how fast a beautiful concert becomes a disaster when nobody plans for a bathroom.”

“You made a touring checklist.”

“An extremely glamorous touring checklist. Also says spare cable and money for gas.”

He hesitated beside the date of his planned concert. “I said yes before asking whether they'd already booked another singer.”

“Then call.”

Greg found the volunteer's number and asked about the schedule. Someone else had booked the afternoon. He didn't demand priority because he was known in another world; he offered an evening set or help with sound if there was room.

When he hung up, his smile was crooked with relief. “Look at that. Being the guy with a guitar doesn't mean I have to be the center of the show.”

He tried to turn the sentiment into a lyric, forgot the rhyme halfway through, and laughed at himself.

Then the van's fuel light caught his eye.

“Speaking of glamorous,” he said, “we should buy gas before I accidentally make this a walking tour.”

I laughed so hard I had to lean against him. He kissed the top of my head, quick and affectionate, and let the old letter remain exactly what it was: a piece of his past, not a script for every choice we made next.


We drove home with the new map folded carefully beside the old note. We didn't cover the past. We made room for it to travel without choosing our destination.

At home Greg placed the note in his song notebook rather than hiding it in the glovebox again.

Before he closed the notebook, he showed me the back of the old paper.

There was a tiny penciled list: a place to sleep, enough money for fuel, one person he could call without rehearsing an apology. He'd crossed out the third line and written it again.

"I didn't remember that part," he said.

"What do you think it meant?"

"That I used to think needing somebody made me a burden."

I rested my hand beside his, not on the paper.

"Do you still think it?"

"Some days. Less often when I ask and get a real answer."

He took a breath.

"Can I ask you for next weekend? Not forever. Just a day."

"Yes. Let's check the calendar before we decide which day."

We did. The Sunday afternoon was free. He wrote it beside the Starwake performance, with enough time between the entries that a delayed crossing wouldn't ruin both plans.

It wasn't a perfect promise.

It was one we understood.

Greg closed the notebook and put it on the shelf where he kept the music he was still working on. The old note had stopped being a secret instruction and become part of a story he was willing to read again.

The map went on the wall.

The first place marked on it was home.

The second was a question mark.
